beats.text: See, there is a school in Delhi, and the coordinator is Asha madam. Delhi's air is sometimes very bad. The tiny dust is measured as PM2.5, and ninety-one or more is called Poor. On a Poor day, children should not stand outside. So every evening she must decide: tomorrow morning, will six hundred children stand outside for assembly, or stay indoors? For that, she needs a guess of tomorrow's PM2.5.

beats.text: Now, she has two ways to guess. Way one, her old method, persistence: look at today's reading and say tomorrow will be the same. It is free. Way two, a small machine-learning model called Ridge, which looks at today, and the last three, seven and fourteen days. So the whole project asks one question: is the model really better than the free method? Because if not, why keep the computer?

beats.text: Let's see it on a toy town, with twenty-two made-up readings. Each row is a question: today is this, what is tomorrow? Fourteen rows are study rows, seven are sealed. Ridge learns only from the study rows, and finds a rule: tomorrow equals zero point three times today, plus sixty-five. Basically, a very high day is usually followed by a lower one. The old method cannot know that.

beats.text: A good student does not only count marks. She opens the answer sheet. Which days did the model lose most? In the toy, the air suddenly cleaned up overnight, and nothing in today's number warned about it. In a long smog spell, Ridge guessed too low. These are patterns, so the ten worst days go into the report as failure cases.

beats.text: So, basically, as Java developers, this should feel familiar. The test set is data you never touch while developing. The pass marks are acceptance criteria written first. The model file is the build the service loads, and the model card is the README. DAF-18 is not about making the model better. It is about testing it once, and reporting honestly, even if the result is bad. DAF-18 done. Next: DAF-19, the live service.
